topics.name: The blow-up statements
topics.description: Smooth solutions, breakdown on space and on the torus, and the theorems that state them (Theorem 1.1, Theorem 7.1).

topics.name: The fractional extension
topics.description: The authors' separate extension with dissipation exponent between 1 and 5/4, outside the classical paper.

topics.name: Heat flow and mild solutions
topics.description: The heat semigroup, the bilinear Duhamel term, mild solutions, restarting and uniqueness (§3).

topics.name: Recurrent profiles
topics.description: Self-similar time-periodic profiles, their slices and orbits, and weak profiles read as physical fields (§2, §4.1, §7.11).

topics.name: Monodromy and the correction
topics.description: The period map, its compact-plus-small splitting, the spectral projection and the fixed point that corrects a profile to an exact solution (§4).

topics.name: Passing to the torus
topics.description: The solenoidal cutoff, periodization and the periodic right inverse that move the construction onto the torus (§5–6).

topics.name: From certificate to profile
topics.description: Certificate data, the free operator, convection, held solutions and the smoothing of the weak profile they produce (§7).

topics.name: The coercive multiplier estimate
topics.description: The multiplier, its five density coefficients and lower bound, and the a priori estimate it gives (Appendix B.1 and B.2).

topics.name: Encoded cell data
topics.description: The finitely represented inputs: coordinates and harmonics, the profile representation, splines and jets, physical cells, rows, weights and potentials.

topics.name: Reduction to the quarter plane
topics.description: Symmetry reduction of the density to the meridian quarter plane (B.3).

topics.name: Cells, traces and tails
topics.description: Integrability, the common vector of unknowns, resolved modes, the tail budget and the exterior estimate (B.4).

topics.name: Angular and ray-exterior tests
topics.description: The angular inequalities, the pointwise test and the integrated test on ray exteriors (B.5 and B.6).

topics.name: The matrix tree lower bound
topics.description: The tree conditions on the cell matrices and the passage from all cells to the global inequality (B.7 and B.8).

topics.name: Changing the profile
topics.description: Bounds for moving estimates from the reference field to the actual profile (B.9).

topics.name: The adjoint pairing and its error
topics.description: The quadratic adjoint pairing, the azimuthal dual norm and the linear adjoint error with potentials and pins (B.10 to B.12).

topics.name: The offset and the certificate
topics.description: Enclosing the constant, linear and quadratic offset, and the fifteen fields of CellSystemCondition that make the data a certificate (B.13 and B.14).

section_aids.1 Introduction: The current Theorem 1.1 begins with a nonzero smooth recurrent similarity profile and constructs finite-time solutions with quantitative blow-up and profile-error estimates. The linked whole-space and periodic implications instead conclude nonexistence of a global smooth solution in specified classes. Their profile premise adds second-derivative and pressure-gradient decay; Remark 1.2 explicitly supplies only the extra velocity regularity. The periodic excluded class allows nonperiodic pressure. The certificate implication belongs to an earlier rectangular formulation and remains conditional on its estimates. Read each comparison as a statement about the particular linked assertion: a definition of a target is not a proof of it, and an implication from certificate bounds is not a supplied numerical certificate.
section_aids.2 Outline of the proof: The whole-space construction represents $\dot H^1_{\rm div}$ by weighted Fourier states, reconstructs $L^6$ velocities and formulates Navier–Stokes through a Bochner integral equation. The transfer assertion chooses a nearby datum in each dense linear subspace and gives a decaying rescaled error. It does not retain Proposition 2.1’s conclusion for every prescribed nearby datum or its fixed finite-dimensional correction space. The regularity theorem works on closed time intervals and gives an unspecified energy bound there, without stating energy nonincrease or one bound on the full half-open lifespan. The periodic target records an unbounded mild curve in the inhomogeneous, possibly nonzero-mean, unit-torus $H^1$ space; the quantitative rates and local profile comparison of Proposition 2.2 are absent from that target.
section_aids.3 Preliminaries: The formal development constructs the solenoidal homogeneous $H^1$ space through gradient-weighted Fourier classes, establishes heat and dilation laws and the bilinear estimate, and proves the Duhamel continuity, restart and uniqueness results used later. Its compactness theorem is stated first for first inputs in the linear span of smooth compactly supported solenoidal fields, a dense class. Its weak-to-mild implication assumes smooth decaying slices and $L^2$-continuous differences, unlike Lemma 3.6. On the torus it uses an inhomogeneous $H^1$ space of period one with unrestricted mean; the bilinear bound is stated for $0<\tau\le1$. These differences must be retained when comparing with the paper’s homogeneous mean-zero spaces at arbitrary period. A numbered display may combine several clauses, and a theorem proving one clause does not establish the entire display.
section_aids.4 The equation linearized about $u^*$: The formal development represents the profile in $\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}$ and works on short rescaled time intervals. Its interval linearization has a genuine inverse once the interaction norm is at most $1/4$; the product over a similarity period differs compactly from a free operator of norm at most $e^{-S/4}$. A real finite-rank spectral splitting, a lift into a dense class of data and a normalized forced recurrence then provide a bounded right inverse for the sequence of interval equations. The nonlinear correction is also stated for such sequences, with endpoint matching and separate residual and datum bounds. The paper presents these constructions on the global weighted spaces $C_\kappa([0,1);X)$. The linked formal statements do not themselves state all of the paper's global weighted estimates, the change from a global source to the forcing of Lemma 4.6, or the identification of the short-interval product with the unsplit trajectory. Those correspondences must be checked separately. The profile-to-orbit step assumes decay through two spatial derivatives and of the pressure gradient, beyond the displayed assumptions (1.3).
section_aids.5 Blow-up on $\\mathbb R^3$: The formal development constructs a solenoidal cutoff through the radial vector potential and proves the support and inner-agreement properties used in §5. Its estimates are stated for a fixed cutoff about $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$, then rescaled to similarity coordinates: the outer radius is $1/(8\sqrt{T-t})$. The squared $L^2$ bound has linear growth in that radius for $0<T-t\le1$, while the exported gradient-error conclusion is qualitative smallness as $T-t\to0$; it does not retain the paper’s uniform $Cr^{-1/2}$ estimate for every independent physical radius. The physical profile is proved mild on $[0,1)$ from its similarity-time mild equation. Correction is carried out through a sequence of interval equations. The final transfer assertion selects a nearby datum in any prescribed dense linear subspace and gives convergence to the profile after similarity rescaling; its quantifiers do not retain Proposition 2.1’s conclusion for every prescribed nearby datum with one correction space and uniform constants.
section_aids.6 Blow-up on the torus: The formal construction starts on the unit torus with the inhomogeneous solenoidal $H^1$ norm and permits a nonzero mean. The paper first works on a torus of period $L$ with the mean-zero homogeneous norm. Accordingly, the formal transplant identity contains the additional term $\mu\|g\|_2^2$. Time is divided into intervals with scales $\mu_n=T\lambda^n$; the cutoff residual and correction are estimated in supremum norms on the normalized intervals. Local restriction records three $L^2$ derivative entries and an $L^6$ value entry in a maximum norm, allowing tuples without derivative compatibility. The heat comparisons yield arbitrarily small errors for sufficiently small scale on the specified compact time ranges, without the explicit powers of $L$ in Lemma 6.1. Two localized operator comparisons transfer an exact right inverse, after which the corrected intervals are joined. The final mild-solution assertion retains smooth periodic initial data and finite-time unboundedness of the periodic norm; it does not state Proposition 2.2’s two-sided blow-up rate or local estimate relative to the self-similar profile.
section_aids.7 From a certificate to a profile: Section 7 assumes approximate profiles, forcing and constraint fields, and quantitative estimates, then derives a weak profile. The formal development represents the velocities in homogeneous Sobolev spaces and the forcing over a normalized period in $L^2$; weak equations use solenoidal test fields. Its certificate asks for global joint $C^1$ dependence on parameter, time and space, supplied weak Hessians and operator-norm decay bounds, and it permits $m=1$ when the paper selects $m=2$. The parameter argument solves the nonlinear correction at each parameter and then uses a finite-dimensional fixed point, whereas the paper uses a joint weak-topology fixed point. The final existence implications do not retain all the information in Theorem 7.1: the selected parameter, quantitative approximation, specified period, identity twist and full prescribed symmetry set are not all part of their conclusions. These implications remain conditional on the certificate hypotheses.
section_aids.Appendix A Proofs of the lemmas of Secti: The formal development proves the abstract mild-solution estimates for a strongly continuous contraction semigroup and a symmetric bilinear operator with the bound $C\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$, including integrability and continuity of Duhamel terms, restarting and uniqueness. Its uniqueness proof uses short intervals; the paper's proof uses an exponentially weighted norm. In the whole-space realization, a continuous mild curve from smooth compactly supported solenoidal data has smooth velocity and pressure on each closed finite time interval, with the momentum equation stated on its interior and equality to the given velocity at every time almost everywhere in space. This statement gives a finite energy bound on the interval; it does not state the energy nonincrease printed in Lemma 2.3. The linked torus results use the unit torus with inhomogeneous $H^1$ norm and allow the constant mode; the paper's corresponding estimates use the zero-mean homogeneous space and arbitrary spatial period.
section_aids.Appendix B Certificates in the formaliza: Appendix B specifies finite representations and conditions sufficient for a certificate. The formal development derives regularity and weak derivatives from the representation, proves multiplier and cell implications, treats unresolved harmonics and exterior regions, and assembles finite-dimensional matrix inequalities. The remaining profile-change, adjoint and offset estimates reduce to specified norm and pairing budgets. A finite representation does not itself verify those budgets: pointwise bounds, integral bounds, positive pivot conditions and matrix comparisons remain assumptions. Some auxiliary statements use broader classes and everywhere-defined derivatives or integrals; for these, the conventions and the separate hypotheses that justify the usual analytic interpretation must be stated. The final cell theorem assumes all fifteen groups of conditions and concludes nonexistence of global smooth solutions in the stated whole-space energy class and for periodic velocity on the unit torus. It supplies no numerical certificate satisfying the conditions.
section_aids.Appendix C The computation of the approx: The linked formal statements describe classes of finite harmonic fields, their radial phases, symmetry and joining conditions, and algebraic or continuum identities used in the linearized equation. They also describe admissible forcing modes and multiplier weights. These are conditions on supplied fields and numbers. They do not carry out the continuation, Newton iteration, flexible GMRES solves, mesh refinement or optimization reported in Appendix C, and they do not supply the particular field with $\varkappa=19$ and $\bar S\approx0.36$. The harmonic label must be converted to its time and azimuthal frequencies before comparing rotating-frame formulas; the radial phase also has a rate parameter whose normalization must be matched. The formalization contains the conditional reductions from certificate data, while the numerical certificate and the rigorous computation verifying its inequalities are absent.
